Why the Minimum Wage Is Bad at Reducing Poverty | Chris Edwards

In fact, relatively few minimum wage workers live in poor households. In a new study, Burkhauser and I examine Census data, and find that workers earning between $7.25 and $10.10 per hour—workers who would be directly affected by [a] proposed federal minimum wage increase—overwhelmingly live in non-poor households. We find that only 13 percent of workers who would be affected live in poor households, while nearly two-thirds live in households with incomes over twice the poverty line, and over 40 percent live in households with incomes over three times the poverty line. Other research suggests that poor single-female headed households make up less than 5 percent of all affected workers.

Now that's an interesting fact.

It's misleading. The US poverty line has not kept pace with reality. For instance the poverty line for a family of 4 with 2 children in the US is $24,036.

I think it should be intuitively clear that's fairly ridiculous. Now in comparing that previous years (I chose 1974), it gets even more absurd. The current poverty level has not even kept up with inflation. Pair this against the fact that many critical industries - housing, healthcare, education, and insurance just to name a few - have increased in cost far faster than inflation and it becomes clear that the poverty wage is being kept artificially low. Why? I'd speculate it's a political attempt to avoid showing the fact that the wealthiest nation in the world ironically has more of their population living in poverty than nearly any other developed country.

Furthermore, our economy today is increasingly dominated by very low wage jobs. Here are the official wage data from the BLS. Sort that table by employment. The median wages for the top 3 industries, which account for about 50 million employees are $15.96, $12.34, and $9.41. What this means is that many households are going to have people working for very low wages. So when you speak of something like people earning $7.25 to $10.10 you're speaking about a huge chunk of the US.

This article says only 13% of the affected live in poor households, which they are defining in terms of the federal poverty standards. Put in light of the information I shared above this makes perfect sense as the national poverty rate, by political standards, is 14.5% and it's low enough that somebody working a minimum wage job technically is often not going to be in poverty even if he's supporting a family off of it. Thus it's not particularly surprising to see the percent affected fall slightly below the national poverty rate.
